Essentially a website (Judicial Watch - Original Story) used 2 Freedom of Information Act requests (Request 1, and Request 2) to obtain IRS documents that detailed communication between higher ups in the IRS (including Lois Lerner, the IRS Director at the time), the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) discussing the current tax-exempt status for conservative leaning 501c charity organizations. These types of organizations remain tax-free with the requirement that they do not focus mainly on political activism, they can dabble, but it cannot be their main focus. The communication seems to indicate that there was a concern in the IRS that certain groups under this umbrella were too political to qualify for this 501c classification and so these IRS officials began to communicate with one another (and possibly officials within the DOJ and FBI) about possible ways to legally engage with these groups to either stop their activities or to remove their 501c classification, thus requiring them to pay taxes and extensible hurting their conservative political activities. Now, while this isn't really that bad, if true it demonstrated a targeted effort from within the IRS aimed at a specific group of people/organization based on political affiliation which is not how the IRS is supposed to be run (i.e. it should be political affiliation agnostic and just run itself like a business). The real problems are rooted in the way that the departments colluded (allegedly) to get technically classified information through less than legitimate channels, including the private tax documentation for these groups, which if true was obtained illegally.

The question then becomes who know what and when, this combined with some questionable hard drive/email management has raised question that have yet to fully be answered.

Please, though keep in mind that as an ELI5, many details are glossed over here and there are more sources out on the web that you can seek our and evaluate on your own.

As others have mentioned, the Arch Wiki is the best source of information. To be specifiec, I suggest:

  • installation guide
  • general recommendations

As an Arch user, and a believer in the Arch Way, I can tell you that while there are alternatives to the traditional CLI installation method, namely Antergos which is pure arch, and Manjaro which is Arch-based, but maintains it's own repos, I cannot in good faith recommend that you use either as your first Arch experience. While Manjaro tries to be Ubuntu+Pacman, Antergos is more suitable for experienced Arch users comfortable with the CLI install method, but who cannot be bothered to do it by hand. Ultimately, Arch is about control, and providing a GUI would reduce the end user's choice on how they want to use their system. I for one would prefer to manually select and install system components, as most "easy" installers got a lot wrong in my book.

At the very least, I would encourage you to do your first install using the official method on the Arch wiki. An understanding of the install process is an important part of being able to maintain and utilize an Arch system. However, once you have a good understanding of the install process, I suggest Evo/Lution, which includes an automated curses-based installer, and makes things about as fast and easy as they can be without the installer making assumptions.

If you are still dead set on not doing a CLI install, Arch may simply not be for you. That is quite all right, and nothing to feel bad about. The beauty of Linux is the choice it offers. If you are looking for a good, GUI-based distro other than Ubuntu, I would look into the following:

  • Debian - a classic; tried and trusted; excellent GUI and CLI installers on the CD; supports many DEs out of the box
  • Fedora - made from the open-source components of RHEL; uses the rpm package manager
  • Mageia - an up and coming distro forked from Mandriva; shows promise
  • openSUSE - another tried and true distro; one of the best pre-baked KDE setups available

If none of these strike your fancy, check out distrowatch!

EDIT 1: I almost forgot. If you are a visual person, you may appreciate the friendly interactive shell as opposed to BASH.

Intellectual engineers Aaron (Shane Carruth) and Abe (David Sullivan) build and sell error-checking technology with the help of their friends Robert (Casey Gooden) and Phillip (Anand Upadhyaya).
